title: Quashawam
summary: Quashawam was a Montaukett sunksquaw whose diplomacy and family testimony shaped land disputes across Long Island. Her story connects captivity and ransom with leadership, annual payments, the Gardiner family, and the defense of Montaukett interests.
content:
Quashawam’s life and leadership

Quashawam was a seventeenth-century Montaukett sunksquaw, the daughter of Wyandanch and Wuchikittawbut. Named agreements document her leadership from February 1664 through the land testimony recorded in June 1666. Her birth date is unknown; Ninigret reported her dead in July 1669.4 5 9

Her public career links the Montaukett homeland with Shinnecock, Jamaica, the Nissequogue country, and colonial courts. She appears as a leader with family land interests and continuing claims to payment, rather than only as the daughter rescued from captivity.4 5 9

1653–1654: captivity, family, and ransom

War with the Eastern Niantic leader Ninigret brought captivity to Wyandanch’s daughter and other Montauketts. Thomas James’s letter of September 6, 1654 describes Wyandanch’s urgent efforts to forward a ransom delayed through Thomas Stanton. James asked John Winthrop Jr. to intervene.1 2

Gardiner’s later account described his own assistance in recovering the captives. The family’s July 1659 deed also acknowledged help with their daughter and friends. These records connect the ransom to a continuing relationship involving counsel, debt, gratitude, and land.1 2

A mother and brother in the same political world

Her mother and brother Wyancombone marked the July 14, 1659 family deed with Wyandanch. After his death, both appear in the August 1660 Montauk transaction. In December 1662, Wuchikittawbut answered questions about her deceased son’s age, and in January 1663 she was still demanding the whale payments due under a beach agreement.2 3

Quashawam’s later leadership followed this history of family participation. The surviving records do not support compressing her mother’s and brother’s deaths into a single event in 1662.2 3

February 11, 1663/64: an agreement with the Shinnecocks

The Southampton records preserve a league between Quashawam and Shinnecock representatives. It recognized her authority and obligations, addressed tribute and conflict, and described a succession involving Awansamaug, a son of the Corchaug sachem, Ponoqt, and descendants of Quashawam and Wyandanch.4

The agreement also directed Awansamaug to reside at Shinnecock in the coming summer and connected payment of forty pounds with release from the remaining fire debt. Quaquashaug, Iaskhonse, Accabaco, and Appanch marked it with Quashawam. Leadership, family succession, and colonial financial demands were joined in the same document.4

On the same day, a separate authorization empowered John Scott to demand payment for lands bought but not paid for and to conduct further land business. Its broad language gave Scott considerable power over transactions made in her name.4

1664–1665: Jamaica, annual payments, and Montauk

A February 25, 1663/64 Jamaica transaction included an order for twelve looking glasses to be delivered to Quashawam. The episode connected her family’s claims with Scott’s business far to the west.8

June 7, 1665: payment still owed to Wyandanch’s heir

A Southold court order required East Hampton to continue the annual twenty-five-shilling payment associated with Wyandanch’s agreement with John Ogden. The beneficiary was his daughter and heir. Later transfer of the settlers’ interest did not simply erase the obligation to her.6

The payment history ties Quashawam to the Quogue and western Southampton lands, as well as to Montauk. It offers a concrete example of a Native family pursuing benefits that continued after an original conveyance.6

October 1665: negotiating with Governor Nicolls

Meetings with Governor Richard Nicolls ended the superior-sachem claim and settled important Montauk boundary and land-use questions. The October 4 agreement recognized Montaukett interests east of Fort Pond, addressed cattle grazing and crop damage, and restricted future sales to East Hampton residents. In May 1668, Nicolls confirmed that this agreement remained in force and that conflicting arrangements made through Scott were void.8 7

1665–1666: Nasseconset’s claim and family testimony

Richard Smith’s account of his dispute with Nasseconset records a meeting with Quashawam. She acknowledged earlier transfers involving her father and brother but could not produce a written document settling Smith’s claim. Smith subsequently paid Nasseconset and Catawump and obtained the deed dated May 4, 1665.5

A separate statement recorded on June 22, 1666 places family memory at the heart of the land history. Pauquatoun described Wyandanch’s grandmother living on Cattawamnuck land. Quashawam said that sachems related to her parents and Tackapousha had interests there and had passed them to her father to dispose of, with part of the payment to go to them.5

The statements preserve overlapping claims and different accounts of past arrangements. Quashawam’s contribution makes kinship and shared compensation visible within a dispute often told only through English founders and patents.5

Her later memory

The romantic name Heather Flower and the wedding-night captivity story developed in later writing; the contemporary documents used here identify her through family relationships and, from 1664, as Quashawam. Her leadership should be remembered alongside the captivity story.8

A contested succession

In July 1669, Ninigret reported Wyandanch’s daughter dead while asserting authority over the Montauketts. That November, Cockenoe and other Montaukett leaders rejected his tribute claim. The community’s political life continued after Quashawam’s final appearance.9 4

Her career connects with Weany and the wider history of Indigenous women’s leadership: women signing agreements, asserting inherited interests, and taking part in disputes that shaped Long Island’s colonial landscape.9 4

why_this_matters: Quashawam makes Native women's leadership visible in Long Island records that are often told only through male sachems and colonial deed makers. Her biography also shows how colonial governments tried to simplify Native authority for land transactions, while Native kinship, diplomacy, and community responsibility were more complex.
activity_update_summary: Expanded historical context, family and land connections, linked references, and dated Historic Moments.
